claims.claim_text: The model was run thousands of times to test how social signals, money, and patronage shape the canon.
claims.evidence_quote: I ran this thousands of times under different conditions.
claims.reasoning: Source confirms thousands of runs and the combined-effect aim; money/patronage are the tested resource factors.

claims.claim_text: Model design: producers, consumers, and gatekeepers, with quality and capital drawn independently.
claims.evidence_quote: three types of agents: producers ... consumers ... and gatekeepers
claims.reasoning: Source states all three agent types and independent quality/capital draws.

claims.claim_text: Each producer gets a random quality score and an independently drawn capital score, so being wealthy does not make you talented.
claims.evidence_quote: Being wealthy doesn't make you talented.
claims.reasoning: Directly restates source's random quality, independent capital, and uncorrelated wealth/talent.

claims.claim_text: Producers with more capital get more exposure, and consumers form opinions from quality, mere exposure, and social signals.
claims.evidence_quote: Consumers form opinions based on actual quality plus the mere exposure effect plus social signals.
claims.reasoning: Matches source sentence on capital-driven exposure and the three opinion inputs.

claims.claim_text: Success feeds back into more exposure, and after many rounds some producers achieve canonical status.
claims.evidence_quote: Success feeds back into more exposure (cumulative advantage).
claims.reasoning: Source states the feedback loop and that some producers reach canonical status after many rounds.

claims.claim_text: Each run took about two minutes with 1,000 producers and 10,000 consumers, parallelized across CPU cores.
claims.evidence_quote: about two minutes with 1,000 producers and 10,000 consumers
claims.reasoning: All quantities and the parallelization detail match source exactly.

claims.claim_text: The author ran 360+ runs per condition for the main experiments, with formal power analysis to check sample sizes.
claims.evidence_quote: ran 360+ per condition for the main experiments, with formal power analysis
claims.reasoning: Source states 360+ per condition and formal power analysis verbatim.

claims.claim_text: Experiment 1: visible social influence weakens the quality-success link.
claims.evidence_quote: Does social influence weaken the quality-success link? Yes.
claims.reasoning: Source answers yes to this exact question.

claims.claim_text: When listeners could see others' consumption, the quality-success correlation dropped significantly (p < 0.0001 across 360 runs per condition).
claims.evidence_quote: drops significantly (p < 0.0001 across 360 runs per condition)
claims.reasoning: p-value, direction, and run count all match source.

claims.claim_text: In a world where nobody could see what anyone else was listening to, quality would be a moderately good predictor of success.
claims.evidence_quote: quality would be a moderately good predictor of success.
claims.reasoning: Verbatim restatement of the source's counterfactual claim.

claims.claim_text: In our world of charts, recommendations, and trending labels, the link gets weaker.
claims.evidence_quote: in a world with charts, recommendations, and "trending" labels (our world), the link gets weaker.
claims.reasoning: Direct paraphrase preserving the 'our world' scope and weakening of the link.

claims.claim_text: A mediocre work that gets lucky early can ride social proof to stardom.
claims.evidence_quote: A mediocre work that gets lucky early can ride social proof to stardom
claims.reasoning: Verbatim restatement with the hedge 'can' preserved.

claims.claim_text: An equally good work that starts slow may never recover.
claims.evidence_quote: may never recover
claims.reasoning: Verbatim restatement preserving the modal 'may never'.

claims.claim_text: Every Top 40 chart, Customers Also Bought widget, and view count is a form of social influence pushing us away from independent judgment.
claims.evidence_quote: systematically pushes us away from independent judgment
claims.reasoning: Matches source's 'every' enumeration and push away from independent judgment.

claims.claim_text: The measurement trap: popularity is used as a proxy for quality, then optimized for, then forgotten as a proxy.
claims.evidence_quote: use popularity as a proxy for quality, then optimize for the proxy, then forget it was a proxy.
claims.reasoning: Exact restatement of the source's proxy sequence.

claims.claim_text: Experiment 2: holding talent constant and reshuffling only resources produces almost entirely different canons.
claims.evidence_quote: Almost entirely different canons from just reshuffling money.
claims.reasoning: Source holds talent constant, reshuffles resources, and reports almost entirely different canons.

claims.claim_text: The counterfactual distance was 0.88 on a 0-to-1 scale, where 0 means identical canons and 1 means completely different ones.
claims.evidence_quote: counterfactual distance was 0.88 on a 0-to-1 scale
claims.reasoning: Value 0.88 and both scale endpoints match source.

claims.claim_text: Only the top 10% of talent had a meaningful shot at fame regardless of funding, and even then only about one in four.
claims.evidence_quote: top 10% of talent ... about 1 in 4
claims.reasoning: Both the 10% and one-in-four figures match source exactly.

claims.claim_text: For everyone in the 50th to 90th percentile of quality, canonical status was effectively a lottery.
claims.evidence_quote: 50th to 90th percentile of quality ... effectively a lottery
claims.reasoning: Percentile range and lottery characterization match source.

claims.claim_text: This is the simulation equivalent of the Haydn question: excellence alone is not enough when the exposure pipeline is narrow.
claims.evidence_quote: excellence alone isn't enough when the exposure pipeline is this narrow
claims.reasoning: Matches source's Haydn-question framing and the 'narrow pipeline' conclusion.

claims.claim_text: Had the Esterházys hired someone else, Haydn would very likely be one of the hundreds of forgotten composers.
claims.evidence_quote: If the Esterházys had hired someone else, Haydn would very likely be one of the hundreds of forgotten
claims.reasoning: Names, hedge 'very likely', and 'hundreds of forgotten' all preserved.

claims.claim_text: Experiment 3: unequal money distorts the canon more than herd behavior.
claims.evidence_quote: Turning off social influence barely helps. But equalizing starting resources jumps ...
claims.reasoning: Source's comparison concludes capital inequality matters more than social influence.

claims.claim_text: Quality-canon correlation by condition: full model 0.32, no social influence 0.35, equal capital 0.46, quality only 0.46.
claims.evidence_quote: Full model ... 0.32 ... No social influence ... 0.35 ... Equal capital ... 0.46 ... Quality only ... 0.46
claims.reasoning: All four correlations and their condition labels match source exactly.

claims.claim_text: Turning off social influence barely helps, but equalizing starting resources jumps the quality-canon correlation by 44%.
claims.evidence_quote: equalizing starting resources jumps the quality-canon correlation by 44%
claims.reasoning: The 44% figure and both effect directions match source.

claims.claim_text: The biggest distortion is not that audiences follow trends; it is that some artists never get heard in the first place.
claims.evidence_quote: The biggest distortion isn't that audiences follow trends. It's that some artists never get heard
claims.reasoning: Preserves both the negation and the contrasted cause exactly.

claims.claim_text: Capital gates access to the exposure pipeline, and everything downstream of that is noise amplification.
claims.evidence_quote: Capital gates access to the exposure pipeline, and everything downstream of that is noise amplification.
claims.reasoning: Verbatim restatement of the source causal claim.

claims.claim_text: The modern mapping: the problem is not that people blindly follow Spotify playlists, but that only major-label artists get on them.
claims.evidence_quote: only major-label artists get on those playlists to begin with
claims.reasoning: Both the negation and the 'only major-label' scope are preserved.

claims.claim_text: Experiment 4: a stylized Vienna run used 300 composers, a handful of very wealthy patrons, strong word-of-mouth, and no recording technology.
claims.evidence_quote: 300 composers, a handful of very wealthy patrons, strong word-of-mouth, no recording technology
claims.reasoning: The 300 count and all four setup features match source.

claims.claim_text: Its counterfactual distance was 0.97, near maximum, with only 2.5% of canonical composers shared between any two alternate histories.
claims.evidence_quote: distance was 0.97, near maximum. Only 2.5% of canonical composers were shared
claims.reasoning: Both 0.97 and 2.5% figures match source exactly.

claims.claim_text: Rewinding to 1750 and randomly reassigning court positions would make the names we teach almost entirely different.
claims.evidence_quote: rewind to 1750 and randomly reassign which composers got which court positions
claims.reasoning: Year 1750, court positions, and 'almost entirely different' all match source.

claims.claim_text: The winners were very likely excellent, since you had to be good to compete for a court position.
claims.evidence_quote: The winners in our timeline were very likely excellent. You had to be good to compete
claims.reasoning: Both the 'very likely excellent' hedge and the competition reason match.

claims.claim_text: Dozens of equally excellent composers were lost to history because they drew the short straw in the patronage lottery.
claims.evidence_quote: dozens of equally excellent composers were lost to history because they drew the short straw
claims.reasoning: Verbatim restatement preserving quantity 'dozens' and the lottery cause.

claims.claim_text: Manufacturing taste means the winners were not bad, but the losers were not meaningfully worse.
claims.evidence_quote: Not that the winners were bad. That the losers weren't meaningfully worse.
claims.reasoning: Both negations preserved exactly from the source definition.

claims.claim_text: Robustness: the results held with every parameter varied by ±50%.
claims.evidence_quote: I varied every parameter by ±50%
claims.reasoning: ±50% matches; robustness framing is confirmed by the source's later robust-direction statement.

claims.claim_text: The single most important factor is how steeply money converts into attention.
claims.evidence_quote: single most important factor is how steeply money converts into attention
claims.reasoning: Verbatim restatement of the source's key-factor claim.

claims.claim_text: If doubling a marketing budget more than doubles the audience, the rich get richer very fast and quality barely matters.
claims.evidence_quote: the rich get richer very fast and quality barely matters
claims.reasoning: Convex condition and both consequences match source.

claims.claim_text: If doubling a budget less than doubles the audience, quality has more room to breathe.
claims.evidence_quote: quality has more room to breathe
claims.reasoning: Concave condition and outcome restated directly from source.

claims.claim_text: In the industry, a major label can buy a front-page Spotify placement reaching 50 million listeners while an independent artist's self-promotion reaches 500.
claims.evidence_quote: front-page Spotify placement reaching 50 million listeners while an independent artist's self-promotion reaches 500
claims.reasoning: Both figures, 50 million and 500, match source exactly.

claims.claim_text: Under such an extremely steep capital-to-exposure curve, quality has very little to do with who becomes famous.
claims.evidence_quote: Our model predicts that under those conditions, quality has very little to do with who becomes famous.
claims.reasoning: Preserves the model-prediction framing and the steep-curve condition.
